lesson.title: Stating the Mean Value Theorem Precisely
lesson.summary: Turning the speedometer intuition into a precise mathematical statement: given the right hypotheses on a closed interval, there is guaranteed to exist at least one point where the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change.
lesson.body:
The Mean Value Theorem states: if f is continuous on the closed interval [a,b] and differentiable on the open interval (a,b), then there exists at least one number c in the open interval (a,b) such that f'(c) = [f(b) - f(a)] / (b - a). Every word in that sentence is load bearing. Continuous on [a,b] includes the endpoints a and b themselves. Differentiable on (a,b) deliberately excludes the endpoints, since a function is allowed to have, say, a corner or a vertical tangent exactly at a or b without breaking the theorem. There exists at least one means the theorem guarantees one or more such points, never zero, but it makes no promise of exactly one; a function can easily have several points where the instantaneous rate matches the average rate.

The quantity on the right side of the conclusion, [f(b) - f(a)] / (b-a), is precisely the average rate of change of f over [a,b]: the change in output divided by the change in input. So the theorem's conclusion can be read as somewhere in the open interval, the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change over the whole interval. Geometrically, [f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a) is also the slope of the secant line connecting the two endpoint points, (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)), so the conclusion says there is a point c where the tangent line to the curve is parallel to that secant line.

Apply the statement to f(x) = x^3 - x on the interval [-1, 2]. This is a polynomial, continuous and differentiable everywhere, so both hypotheses hold automatically on [-1,2]. Compute the two endpoint values: f(-1) = (-1)^3 - (-1) = -1 + 1 = 0, and f(2) = 2^3 - 2 = 8 - 2 = 6. The average rate of change is [f(2) - f(-1)] / [2 - (-1)] = (6 - 0)/3 = 2. The theorem guarantees some c in the open interval (-1, 2) with f'(c) = 2. Since f'(x) = 3x^2 - 1, set 3c^2 - 1 = 2, so 3c^2 = 3, c^2 = 1, giving c = 1 or c = -1. Here is where the open interval wording matters: c = -1 is an endpoint, not a member of the open interval (-1,2), so it does not count; only c = 1 lies strictly inside (-1,2). Checking, f'(1) = 3(1)^2 - 1 = 2, matching the average rate exactly. The theorem is satisfied by exactly one of the two algebraic solutions, and the statement's careful phrasing, in the open interval, is exactly what tells you which root to keep.

This example is worth sitting with, because it shows that the theorem's guarantee of existence is not automatically the same as solve f'(x) equals the average rate and take any root. You solve that equation, then check which root or roots actually fall inside the open interval (a,b); the theorem promises at least one will.
